item.content: When adding a new configuration variable to Flask, register its default in the app's default config dict (flask/app.py), document it in docs/config.rst, add a CHANGES entry, and reference it via current_app.config[...] at the point of use.

Prefer exposing behavior through a config variable (e.g. app.config['JSONIFY_MIMETYPE']) rather than adding a new function parameter or separate API; reviewers expect the simplest config-driven approach.

Flask's jsonify builds its response via current_app.response_class with a mimetype; the default JSON mimetype is 'application/json' and can be overridden for vendor media types like 'application/vnd.api+json'.
When fixing Python 3 encoding issues in file reading, open files in binary mode ('rb') and let compile()/exec handle the encoding declaration; do not assume text-mode open() decodes correctly.

Flask still supports Python 2.6, so avoid syntax/features added in 2.7+ (e.g. str.format with '{}' auto-numbering); use explicit '{0}' placeholders and check flask._compat.PY2 for version-dependent test assertions.
When changing behavior, add a regression test that exercises the bug (e.g. parametrized over multiple source encodings) and add a CHANGES entry referencing the issue number.

When parsing boolean-like environment variables, normalize with .lower() before comparing against string literals like 'false'/'no'/'0'; users may set FLASK_DEBUG=False with Python-style capitalization.
For small behavior fixes, keep the change minimal and targeted (e.g. one-line normalization) rather than restructuring; hidden tests typically check the exact edge case described in the issue.

When parsing a host:port string like SERVER_NAME, use str.partition(':') to split into host and port safely; it returns an empty string for the missing part instead of raising, avoiding tuple-unpacking failures when no port is present.
When reading optional config values, use config.get('KEY') and guard with `if value:` before parsing; accessing config['KEY'] or unpacking its parts can fail when the key is unset or lacks a port.

For fallback chains like host = host or sn_host or default, prefer `or` chaining over nested if/else; it reads cleaner and handles None/empty uniformly, but ensure each candidate is defined (initialize to None) before the chain.

When removing reliance on a request header (e.g. X-Requested-With) for behavior, replace it with a config flag and/or app.debug check, and update the default config value, docs/config.rst, CHANGES, and affected tests in the same change.

When changing a default config value that alters output formatting, update existing tests that assert the old formatted output (e.g. pretty-printed JSON bytes) and set app.debug=True in tests that depend on debug-mode behavior.
Flask's jsonify pretty-printing is controlled by JSONIFY_PRETTYPRINT_REGULAR (default False in newer versions) and app.debug; it no longer inspects request.is_xhr / the X-Requested-With header.

When a CLI or framework silently swallows an exception (e.g. a bare `pass` in an except block), replace it with traceback.print_exc() (or equivalent logging) so users see the error, and add a test that invokes the code path and asserts both the exception message and 'Traceback' appear in output.

When a reviewer says a comment or code is 'not needed anymore since there's some actual code now', remove the stale comment/placeholder rather than leaving it alongside the new implementation; keep the diff focused on the behavior change.

Flask's CLI is built on click's FlaskGroup; create_app failures during command listing/help are caught in list_commands, and CliRunner.invoke captures stdout so traceback output can be asserted in tests.

When catching exceptions to record them before re-raising, use `except BaseException as e:` rather than a bare `except:` with sys.exc_info(); bare except also catches SystemExit/KeyboardInterrupt but obscures intent and reviewers flag it. Re-raise with a bare `raise` to preserve the traceback.

When a fix changes error/exception handling, add a test using pytest.raises for the specific exception type (e.g. KeyboardInterrupt) and assert the internal state that the fix affects (e.g. ctx.preserved and ctx._preserved_exc type), plus a CHANGES entry.
Don't rely on sys.exc_info() inside a bare except to get the exception; prefer `except BaseException as e` so the exception object is directly available and the code is clearer to reviewers.

When adding documentation examples, match the naming and style used in surrounding examples (e.g. use the same app name like `hello` rather than inventing `foo.py`), and prefer installed package names over file names in commands.

Don't assume a single activation script works across shells; virtualenv provides different activate scripts per shell (POSIX `activate`, Windows `activate.bat`), so document each shell's script explicitly.
When a reviewer flags awkward wording or asks for a rephrase, adopt their suggested phrasing verbatim where possible; it reduces further review cycles.

When adding new constructor keyword arguments to a framework class, place them in a sensible position (grouping related ones like host_matching/static_host together), document them in the class docstring with a versionadded note and :param: entries, and add a CHANGES entry referencing the issue number.

Don't use a property like has_static_folder to infer whether the folder actually exists on disk; it only indicates that a static_folder was configured. If existence matters, check the filesystem explicitly, and word comments accordingly.

When a new option has a required companion (e.g. host_matching=True requires static_host when a static_folder is configured), enforce the invariant with an assert or explicit error at construction time and add tests covering both the valid and invalid combinations.

When emitting HTTP headers with multiple related parameters (e.g. Content-Disposition filename and filename*), build the parameter dict conditionally and pass it via **kwargs to headers.add; only include the extended (RFC 2231) parameter when the value is non-ASCII, so ASCII filenames keep a simple filename= header.

HTTP headers are latin-1 only; for non-ASCII attachment filenames use RFC 2231 encoding: filename*=UTF-8''<percent-encoded>, and provide an ASCII fallback filename= (e.g. via unicodedata.normalize('NFKD', ...).encode('ascii', 'ignore')) for older clients.

Don't rely on dict ordering or Werkzeug Headers.add to control the order of Content-Disposition parameters (IE8 requires filename before filename*); since ordering can't be guaranteed across Werkzeug versions, prefer omitting filename* for ASCII names rather than attempting to force order.

In Sphinx docs, wrap prose at 79 characters and use double backticks (``code``) for all inline code, including converter names, config keys, and literals; single backticks are reserved for roles like :meth:.

When editing documentation sections, preserve existing cross-reference roles (:meth:, :func:, :ref:) and section anchors; rewrite prose but keep the semantic markup intact so links and toctree references still resolve.

When a doc edit removes content (e.g. an HTTP method overview), verify no other section or file references it via :ref: or toctree before deleting, and keep the remaining section headings' underline lengths matching the new title text.

When writing tests that set environment variables, use pytest's monkeypatch.setenv rather than mutating os.environ directly, and DRY up repeated assertions over different inputs with @pytest.mark.parametrize listing (input, expected) tuples.
In test assertions, prefer `assert x is None` for None checks and `assert x` / `assert not x` for truthiness rather than `== True` / `== False`; reviewers flag the explicit comparisons as noise.

When testing a helper that builds a response (e.g. make_response), call it directly inside app.test_request_context() and assert on the returned response object's status_code/data/mimetype; don't register a view and go through the test client just to exercise the helper.

When converting unittest examples to pytest in docs, use a yield fixture (setup before `yield`, teardown after) rather than setUp/tearDown methods, and make teardown prose explicit about who cleans up (e.g. 'the pytest fixture closes the file and removes the database') so beginners don't think they must do it manually.

In example code shown in docs, follow PEP-8 import grouping (stdlib, blank line, third-party, blank line, local) and PEP-257 docstrings (complete sentences ending with a period); reviewers treat example code as teaching material and flag these nits even when they'd ignore them in library code.

pytest auto-discovers test files named test_*.py, so docs should instruct placing tests in a tests/ directory with that naming; fixtures are declared with @pytest.fixture and injected by parameter name into test functions.

When appending to a comma-separated HTTP header (e.g. Vary), parse existing values by splitting on ',' and stripping whitespace, compare case-insensitively (h.lower() == value.lower()), and only append if absent; then reassign the whole header with response.headers['Vary'] = ', '.join(values) rather than using headers.add, which would create duplicate header lines.

Don't reach for a regex to split simple delimited header values; a list comprehension with .strip() over header.split(',') is clearer and reviewers will ask you to drop the regex. Also don't make such helpers overridable via module-level constants or config when they're internal one-off logic.

When a helper mutates a response header, write tests that cover: header absent, header already containing the exact value (no duplicate), and header containing other values (value appended in order); assert len(rv.headers.get_all('Vary')) == 1 to catch duplicate header lines.

Don't use `.. sourcecode:: html` (or any language) for blocks that are actually raw HTTP headers; use `.. sourcecode:: none` (or no highlighting) so the block isn't mislabeled, and reviewers will flag the wrong lexer.
Don't link to top-level MDN or vendor landing pages (e.g. developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP); link to the specific header/protocol page so readers land on the relevant reference.

HSTS `preload` is only valid together with `includeSubDomains`; document the directive combinations accordingly (e.g. `max-age=...; includeSubDomains; preload`) rather than listing `preload` standalone.

When parsing a string expression like 'name(args)' from config, use a single regex with named groups (e.g. r'^(?P<name>\w+)(?:\((?P<args>.*)\))?$') and ast.literal_eval on the args wrapped as a tuple; strip trailing commas/spaces with rstrip(' ,') before evaluating so 'a, b,' parses cleanly.

When the same factory-calling logic is needed from multiple entry points (auto-detection and explicit string lookup), extract it into one shared helper (e.g. call_factory(app_factory, script_info, arguments=())) rather than duplicating argument-inspection logic; reviewers explicitly ask for this.
Don't leave docstrings or comments as unfinished fragments (e.g. 'If it is a '); reviewers flag straggling sentences. Write complete sentences and remove placeholder text before submitting.

Don't use tabs for indentation in Python source; reviewers flag it immediately. Use 4 spaces per level, and don't add blank lines before blocks unless the surrounding code style already does so—PEP8 doesn't require it and reviewers may push back on gratuitous whitespace changes.

When a helper builds a URL from a parsed path, prefer str.format with named placeholders (scheme=, netloc=, path=) over positional {0}/{1}/{2}; it makes the fallback logic (url.scheme or url_scheme) self-documenting and avoids miscounting arguments.

Flask's make_test_environ_builder parses the path with werkzeug's url_parse; when the path is a full URL its scheme/netloc override PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME and http_host, so tests can assert eb.url_scheme, eb.host, eb.script_root, and eb.path directly.

When cleaning up a CI config (e.g. .appveyor.yml), move the interpreter path into PATH via an `init:` step (SET PATH=%PYTHON%;%PATH%) and then invoke `python -m ...` everywhere, instead of repeating the full %PYTHON%\python.exe prefix on each command; this removes duplication and makes the config easier to read.

When a CI matrix lists multiple Python versions, keep the entries sorted (e.g. 27, 35, 36) and add a version-printing step (python -c "import sys;sys.stdout.write(sys.version)") so build logs confirm which interpreter actually ran.

Don't assume a CI config change is accepted just because the reviewer says 'lgtm'; hidden tests may still reject it. Verify the config actually parses and that the intended matrix/commands are present before considering the task done.

When introducing a new environment/config flag (e.g. FLASK_ENV) that gates debug features, add a property on the app object (using @property) that derives behavior from the flag, default to the safe value (production), and update all docs that previously told users to set the old flag (FLASK_DEBUG) to reference the new one.

Don't mention old Flask versions or migration notes inline in user-facing docs unless the reviewer asks; it adds confusion. Keep docs focused on current behavior, and don't claim a feature 'kicks in' automatically when it actually requires a separate flag (e.g. debugger only activates with FLASK_DEBUG=1).

Match the surrounding code's indentation and spacing style exactly; don't introduce a visually inconsistent indentation (e.g. double-indenting continuation lines) or remove blank lines between blocks that the existing code uses for readability. Reviewers flag style inconsistencies even in small diffs.

When gating existing implicit behavior behind a new opt-in flag (e.g. subdomain_matching), keep the old behavior reachable via the flag, default to the safe/off value, and update every docstring versionchanged note, docs/config.rst, CHANGES, and tests that relied on the implicit behavior in the same change.

Don't leave unbalanced parentheses or other syntax errors in docstrings/comments; reviewers catch them immediately. Run a quick syntax check (python -m py_compile or flake8) on edited files before submitting.

Flask's subdomain route matching depends on SERVER_NAME being set and url_map.host_matching being False; since 1.0 it must be explicitly enabled with Flask(subdomain_matching=True) rather than being implied by SERVER_NAME.

ssl.SSLContext was added in Python 2.7.9, not 2.7.0; version checks gating SSLContext usage must compare against (2, 7, 9) rather than (2, 7), and the same threshold must be applied consistently in both source and tests.

When a version-gated feature check is wrong, grep for every occurrence of the same version tuple (e.g. sys.version_info < (2, 7)) across source and tests and update them all together; a reviewer comment like 'something is missing here' often means a sibling check or test was left at the old threshold.

Don't assume the issue reporter's claim that 'no additional tests are needed' is correct; when a version threshold changes, update the existing tests that branch on that threshold so they exercise the new boundary, otherwise hidden tests may fail.

When a reviewer questions whether a micro-optimization (e.g. moving a function call) is actually faster, only keep it if you can justify it; otherwise revert that hunk and keep the clearly-correct changes (like moving a call past an early-return branch so it isn't executed on the propagate path).

Don't bundle speculative refactors with a targeted fix; reviewers reject 'trading complexity' changes that aren't backed by profiling. Keep only the change that removes genuinely dead/unnecessary work on a code path.
When a reviewer asks for a grammar fix in a docstring/comment (e.g. 'that return`s` a response'), apply it verbatim in the same change as the code fix.

When a helper like copy_current_request_context delegates to a context object's copy() method, put the actual behavior change in the copy() method (e.g. RequestContext.copy()) rather than in the wrapper, and update the wrapper's docstring to describe the new behavior; reviewers explicitly ask for this placement.

When adding a new optional constructor parameter to a context/state class (e.g. session=None on RequestContext), default it to None so existing call sites keep working, and thread the value through from the copy() method that needs it.

Don't describe passing the same object reference as a 'copy' in docstrings or changelog entries; say 'the current session object is used instead of reloading the original data' so readers aren't misled into thinking a new object is created.

When replacing a locally-defined class with an upstream (dependency) version, keep a thin subclass that only overrides the framework-specific hooks (e.g. `json_module = json`, `on_json_loading_failed`), and bump the minimum dependency version in setup.py plus a CHANGES entry in the same change.

Don't delete tests wholesale when moving behavior to a dependency; keep tests that verify framework-specific integration (e.g. request context / blueprint overrides of flask.json.loads) and only remove tests that purely exercise the upstream library's own behavior.
When a change bumps a dependency version, put the version bump as its own top-of-changelog entry so it's visible, separate from the feature entry that references the issue.

When a reviewer proposes a one-liner (e.g. `next((int(x) for x in (a, b, c) if x is not None), default)`), adopt it but verify the default/fallback semantics: if all candidates are None, decide whether to fall back to a hardcoded default or leave None, and add a test for that all-None case.

Don't use `x or default` for values where 0 (or empty string) is a legitimate value; use explicit `is not None` checks so 0 isn't silently replaced by the default. This applies to ports, timeouts, and other numeric config values.

When a reviewer points out a case the fix misses (e.g. 'SERVER_NAME=<IP>:0 should also work'), extend the fix to cover all equivalent input sources (explicit arg, config-derived value, hardcoded default) and add a parametrized test row for each source, not just the one originally reported.

When converting a factory function into a class that subclasses an upstream class (e.g. werkzeug.test.EnvironBuilder), delegate to the base class for behavior it already provides (JSON serialization, kwargs handling) instead of reimplementing it; override only the framework-specific hooks (e.g. json_dumps to inject app config) and pass remaining *args/**kwargs through to super().__init__.

When deprecating a public function in favor of a new class, keep the old function as a thin wrapper that emits a DeprecationWarning (with the removal version) and delegates to the new class, update internal call sites (e.g. app.test_request_context) to use the class directly, and add a CHANGES entry noting the deprecation and replacement.

Don't keep hand-rolled logic that duplicates what a base class or dependency already handles (e.g. manually converting a 'json' kwarg to 'data' plus content_type when the base EnvironBuilder does it); reviewers will ask you to remove it. Verify the base class's behavior before reimplementing.

When pinning a dependency to an upper bound (e.g. 'Werkzeug>=0.7,<1.0'), keep the existing lower bound and add the upper bound in the same install_requires string; add a CHANGES entry noting the pin so the constraint is visible to users.

Don't over-extend a dependency pin request to unrelated packages (e.g. adding Jinja2<3 when the issue only asks for Werkzeug<1.0); keep the pin scoped to the package named in the issue unless the reviewer explicitly asks for more.

Flask 0.12 is incompatible with Werkzeug 1.0+, so setup.py must constrain Werkzeug to '>=0.7,<1.0'; the lower bound reflects the oldest supported version and the upper bound prevents breakage from the next major release.

When a fix is a one-character/one-token change (e.g. set literal `{...}` to tuple `(...)`), make only that change; don't add extra logic or alternative code paths, since reviewers reject 'having both (especially with different logic)'.
Don't use a set literal for a small fixed sequence of names that will be iterated in priority order (e.g. factory names to try); sets are unordered, so use a tuple to make selection deterministic.

Flask's CLI find_best_app searches for app factory functions by iterating candidate attribute names; the order matters when a module defines both create_app and make_app, so the candidates must be an ordered sequence (tuple), not a set.

Don't delete or move existing tests when adding a new test; reviewers reject diffs that remove unrelated test coverage (e.g. deleting a whole TestJSON class or helper functions from tests/test_helpers.py). Add the new test alongside the existing ones and keep the diff additive.

When testing a JSON encoder's default() behavior, call json.dumps(obj) rather than instantiating the encoder and calling .encode()/.default() directly, since dumps is the typical use case; use plain module-level functions or simple string values instead of defining a class with class attributes when a literal suffices.

Don't add asserts that don't verify meaningful behavior (e.g. asserting a class attribute equals itself or a trivially-true condition); reviewers flag these as unnecessary noise. Each assert should test an observable outcome of the code under test.

When re-adding a deprecated parameter to a function, give it a default of None (e.g. `filename: t.Optional[str] = None`) so existing call sites keep working, and only emit the DeprecationWarning when the value is not None; reviewers explicitly flag a missing `= None`.

Don't guess the stacklevel for warnings.warn in a deprecation shim; stacklevel=2 points at the caller of the deprecated function, which is what users need to see. Higher values (e.g. 3) skip past the caller and are usually wrong unless the warning is emitted from a nested helper.

When deprecating a renamed parameter, document the rename with a `.. versionchanged::` note in the function docstring (e.g. '``path`` replaces the ``filename`` parameter') in addition to the DeprecationWarning and CHANGES entry, so the API history is visible in the docs.

When combining nested prefixes/paths, use `options.get(key) or fallback` rather than `if key in options` so an explicit None value falls through to the fallback; then only concatenate when both parts are non-None, and strip/join with rstrip('/') + '/' + lstrip('/') to avoid double slashes.

Don't write convoluted tests that exercise many features at once to demonstrate a fix; reviewers ask for a minimal test that isolates the reported behavior (e.g. the exact snippet from the issue). Keep the test focused on the prefix combination and add separate cases for overrides.

Flask blueprint nesting combines url_prefix values: a child blueprint's own url_prefix is combined with the parent's, and a url_prefix passed to register_blueprint overrides the child's own value; the combined prefix is threaded through BlueprintSetupState.url_prefix when registering nested blueprints.

Don't mutate shared state (e.g. a blueprint's options dict or a setup state's url_prefix) when computing per-registration values; build a fresh dict/copy for each registration so one parent registration doesn't leak into future ones. Reviewers flag this explicitly.

When fixing nested blueprint prefix combination, handle all three cases explicitly: child has its own url_prefix (combine with parent), register_blueprint passes an override (use it), and neither is set (fall back to the parent's state.url_prefix). Add a test for the parent-only case, not just the combined case.

In Flask's Blueprint.register, bp_options['url_prefix'] must be set for every nested registration; if the child has no url_prefix and no override is given, it must inherit state.url_prefix, otherwise the parent's prefix is silently dropped from the child's routes.

When tightening type annotations on a decorator factory (e.g. returning t.Callable[[F], F] instead of bare t.Callable), also fix the wrapper decorator (e.g. setupmethod) to preserve the wrapped function's type via a TypeVar bound to t.Callable[..., t.Any] and t.cast(F, update_wrapper(...)); otherwise the wrapper erases the new type info and reviewers flag it.

When adding a parameter to a method that forwards to another method via a recorded lambda (e.g. Blueprint.add_url_rule recording s.add_url_rule(...)), pass the new parameter explicitly by keyword in the lambda call; if it was previously accepted via **options, omitting it silently drops it and reviewers flag the bug.

Flask's Scaffold.add_url_rule returns None (it registers the rule), not a Callable; annotate it as -> None. Blueprint.add_url_rule mirrors Flask.add_url_rule's signature including provide_automatic_options, which must be threaded through the recorded lambda.

When a reviewer asks 'why doesn't this use X?' (e.g. request.blueprints instead of a private helper), replace the helper with the existing public API and delete the now-unused private method; don't keep both.

Don't raise a generic exception (e.g. AssertionError via assert) for user-facing invalid input like a duplicate registration name; use ValueError so callers can catch it and the message is meaningful.

When a reviewer says formatting is 'weird' because a line wraps, extract repeated subexpressions (e.g. self.options.get(...) calls) into local variables before building the expression, keeping the line under the wrap limit.

When fixing a static typing annotation for a decorator that wraps user functions (e.g. template_global/template_filter), use t.Callable[..., t.Any] (or the appropriate return type) so any signature is accepted; don't narrow to a fixed argument list, and apply the same fix to sibling annotations (filter, global, test) in one change.

Don't add a new changelog section or bump to an unreleased version for a small fix; add the entry under the existing Unreleased/next-patch section (e.g. 2.0.2) and follow the surrounding entries' issue-link style (:issue:`NNNN`) with no extra blank lines.
Don't wrap plain-English phrases (e.g. 'template global') in double backticks in changelog/docs prose; reserve code formatting for actual identifiers, config keys, and literals.

When a reviewer suggests a set literal (e.g. `for c in {code, None}:`) to deduplicate a small ordered sequence, push back: sets are unordered and iteration order matters here. Instead deduplicate while preserving order, e.g. `[code, None] if code is not None else [None]`, and keep the change minimal.

Don't use a set to deduplicate values that are iterated in priority order (e.g. error handler lookup candidates like [code, None]); the first match wins, so order must be deterministic. Use an explicit conditional list or dict.fromkeys to dedupe while preserving order.

Flask's _find_error_handler iterates candidate codes [code, None] (specific HTTP code first, then the generic None handler) across request.blueprints then None; when the exception has no code, code is None and the list contains None twice, so deduplication must preserve the specific-before-generic order.

When adding async support to a framework dispatch path, wrap the handler call with current_app.ensure_sync(...) at the point of invocation (e.g. View.as_view's view function and MethodView.dispatch_request) rather than adding separate async code paths; add async test view classes and extend the existing parametrized async test with their routes.

Don't classify a change as a feature when the maintainers consider it a bug fix (e.g. async support that was intended for the current release); put the CHANGES entry under the existing Unreleased section as a fix and don't add a new version section.

Flask's app.ensure_sync(func) returns func unchanged for sync callables and wraps coroutine functions with asgiref.sync.async_to_sync; it is the standard hook for making any handler (route, error handler, class-based view method) async-capable.
